mcqs.learning_point: Simplify square roots of perfect-square factors
mcqs.question: Simplify the surd \(\sqrt{72}\) by removing all perfect‑square factors.
mcqs.explanation: 72 = 36 × 2, and 36 is a perfect square (6²). Therefore \(\sqrt{72}=\sqrt{36\times2}=\sqrt{36}\times\sqrt{2}=6\sqrt{2}.\) Options B, C and D either use incorrect factors or miss the perfect‑square extraction.

mcqs.question: What is the sum of \(3\sqrt{5}\) and \(2\sqrt{5}\)?
mcqs.explanation: Surds with the same radicand are like terms. Add the coefficients: 3 + 2 = 5, so \(3\sqrt{5}+2\sqrt{5}=5\sqrt{5}.\) The other options either change the radicand or give an incorrect coefficient.

mcqs.question: Rationalising the denominator of \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\) gives which of the following expressions?
mcqs.explanation: Multiply numerator and denominator by \(\sqrt{3}\): \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{3}}=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{3}.\) This removes the radical from the denominator. Options B, C, D either leave a radical in the denominator or change the value.

mcqs.question: Rationalise the denominator of \(\dfrac{5}{2+\sqrt{3}}\) and write the result in simplest form.
mcqs.explanation: Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate \(2-\sqrt{3}\): \(\dfrac{5}{2+\sqrt{3}}\times\dfrac{2-\sqrt{3}}{2-\sqrt{3}}=\dfrac{5(2-\sqrt{3})}{(2)^2-(\sqrt{3})^2}=\dfrac{5(2-\sqrt{3})}{4-3}=5(2-\sqrt{3})=10-5\sqrt{3}.\) Options B, C, D are either not rationalised or give a different value.

mcqs.question: Simplify \(\dfrac{\sqrt{18}+\sqrt{8}}{\sqrt{2}}\) and choose the correct result.
mcqs.explanation: First, \(\sqrt{18}=\sqrt{9\times2}=3\sqrt{2}\) and \(\sqrt{8}=\sqrt{4\times2}=2\sqrt{2}\). Their sum is \(5\sqrt{2}\). Dividing by \(\sqrt{2}\) gives \(\dfrac{5\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}}=5\). Hence option A is correct; the others are not equal to the simplified value.

mcqs.learning_point: Simplify square roots of perfect-square factors
mcqs.question: A square garden has an area of \(200\,\text{m}^2\). Express the length of each side in simplest surd form.
mcqs.explanation: Side length = \(\sqrt{200}\). Factor 200 as \(100\times2\); 100 is a perfect square (10²). Thus \(\sqrt{200}=\sqrt{100\times2}=10\sqrt{2}.\) Option A gives the simplified surd; option D leaves it unsimplified, while B and C are numerically different.

mcqs.question: Which of the following statements about surd multiplication is correct?
mcqs.explanation: When multiplying surds with the same index, multiply the radicands: \(\sqrt{2}\times\sqrt{3}=\sqrt{2\times3}=\sqrt{6}.\) Options A, B, and D misuse addition/subtraction or give an incorrect radicand, reflecting common misconceptions.

mcqs.question: Why is it necessary to rationalise the denominator of \(\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{5}-\sqrt{2}}\)?

options.A: To eliminate radicals from the denominator and write the expression in standard form
options.C: Because it changes the value of the expression to a whole number
options.D: To introduce the constant \(\pi\) into the expression

mcqs.answer: To eliminate radicals from the denominator and write the expression in standard form
mcqs.explanation: Rationalising removes radicals from the denominator, giving a more convenient and conventional form for further calculations. It does not alter the value of the expression, nor does it affect the numerator size or introduce \(\pi\). Hence option A is correct; the other options describe incorrect reasons.
